title: Junior Clerkship Rotation Learning Objectives
notes: The attached file was a ZIP archive despite its .pdf extension.
Objectives were extracted from all 13 PDF and 2 DOCX guides in the archive.
Whitespace and list formatting were normalized; source wording was otherwise retained as closely as possible.
General objectives and topic/session-level objectives are separated. Page locators refer to physical PDF pages; DOCX locators refer to paragraph indexes.
Case narratives, timetables, assessment instructions, references, and teaching logistics were excluded unless an explicitly labeled learning-objective subsection appeared within them.

Acute Dyspnoea(minutes to hours): Shortness of breath occurring over minutes to hours is caused by a relatively small number of conditions. Attention to clinical information and consideration of these conditions can lead to an accurate diagnosis. Diagnosis permits initiation of therapy that can limit associated morbidity and mortality. Cardiac causes

Myocardial dysfunction (congestive heart failure)
Ischemic/Hypertensive cardiomyopathy ii. Dilated cardiomyopathy (idiopathic, alcoholic, haemochrom atosis) c. Pericardial disease (tamponade and constrictive pericarditis)
Pulmonary causes
Upper airway
Aspiration ii.
Anaphylaxis
Ventilatory pump
Pleura (pneumothorax) ii. Airways (bronchitis, bronchospasm) c. Gas exchange
Pulmonary embolus ii. Pneumonia (viral, bacterial, atypical, fungus) iii. ARDS iv. Vasculitis (Wegener, Goodpasture)
Respiratory control (metabolic acidosis, salicylate toxicity)

Chronic Dyspnoea(weeks to months): Since patients with acute dyspnea require more immediate evaluation and treatment, it is important to differentiate them from those with chronic dyspnea. topic_objectives.topic: Approach to a child with pallor

objectives: Recognize common hematological conditions in children presenting with anemia

Students should understand the etiological classification of anemia.
Poor Production: Nutrient deficiency: Iron deficiency anemia, B12 & folic acid deficiency.
Bone marrow failure: Pure red cell aplasia, Fanconi anemia, acquired aplastic anemia • Bone Marrow infiltration: Leukemia, lymphoma, neuroblastoma, lipid storage disorders.
Increased Destruction (Hemolysis): Hemoglobinopathies: Sickle cell disease & Thalassemia
Enzymopathies: G6PD deficiency, pyruvate kinase deficiency
Membranopathies: Hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis
Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia: DIC, TTP, HUS
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
Sequestrations: e.g. Acute splenic sequestration in SCD
Increase Loss (Hemorrhagic Anemia): Acute blood loss: Road traffic accidents, Trauma
Chronic blood loss: Diaphragmatic hernia, hemorrhoids

Take a detailed history of the pallor, including how it was discovered, onset, course, duration, any treatment given, associated manifestations such as bone aches, swelling of hand/feet, fever, shortness of breath, and abdominal distension. Color of urine and stool, jaundice, easy fatigability, any blood loss from body orifices, and any triggering factors such as certain types of food or medications should be mentioned as negative data. History of simple blood transfusion and/or exchange transfusion should be outlined in detail. Past History: Including neonatal screening for G6PD and hemoglobinopathies; prolonged or recurrent hospital admission. Family history: consanguinity and hematological disorders in siblings or parents Drug history: Iron or multivitamin therapy, hydroxyurea, folic acid, analgesics, chemotherapy or biological agents should be mentioned. Nutritional History: This should be carried out in full detail, including the age of weaning, number of meals, and type of food.

Skin and mucous membranes:

To examine skin and conjunctiva for jaundice in natural light.
To check for any mucocutaneous bleeding tendency, café au lait spots of the skin, or any other abnormalities.
Examination of hands/feet especially in infants with suspected SCD.
Assessment of general condition, associated signs of infections, congenital anomalies, and dysmorphic features.
Detailed examination of lymph nodes.
Cardiac examination: Gallop or hemic murmurs
Chest examination: Any mediastinal masses or signs of consolidation
Abdominal examination: Assessment for organomegaly.
Based on history and physical examination, the student should be able to formulate a list of differential diagnoses and generate a plan of investigations.

topic_objectives.topic: Approach to a child with a bleeding tendency

objectives: Obtain a proper history in a child presenting with bleeding tendency/easy bruising.
Be able to differentiate between non-accidental injury and disorders of hemostasis.
Perform a detailed clinical examination, including general examination, assessment of mucocutaneous bleeding, abdominal examination, and musculoskeletal system examination.
Get a clue from history and examination to differentiate between coagulation and bleeding disorders.
Know when to refer pediatric cases with a significant bleeding tendency.
Plan a stepwise approach of investigations, tailored for each case.
Interpret the results of hematological investigations accurately.
Recognize common hematological conditions in children presenting with bleeding tendency.
Manage acute bleeding episodes in some common pediatric disorders.
Counsel the families effectively.
Bleeding Disorders
Decrease in number:
Decrease production: Bone marrow failure/BM infiltration (leukemia, lymphoma)
Increased destruction:
Immune-mediated (ITP, Evans syndrome)
Non-immune-mediated (microangiopathy: DIC, HUS, TTP)
Ii9) Abnormal Sequestration: Acute splenic sequestration, Kassabach-Merritt syndrome
Platelet dysfunction:
Congenital VWD, Bernard-Soulier syndrome, Glanzmann's,
Acquired: Drugs (Aspirin, NSAIDs)
Vascular disorders
o Ehler Danlos syndrome, scurvey
Coagulation Disorders
Hemophilia, VWD, factor deficiencies, hypofibrinogenemia.
Non-Accidental Injury

Take a detailed history of the bleeding episode, including onset, course, duration, aggravating and relieving factors, recurrence, sites, mucosal involvement, and bleeding from orifices including epistaxis, gingival bleeding, hematemesis, hemoptysis, hematuria, melena, and hematochezia. History of preceding upper respiratory tract infections and any associated manifestations such as fever, pallor, and bone aches should be considered. History of surgical challenges, post-procedural bleeding, post-circumcision bleeding, bleeding after dental extraction, bleeding from umbilical stump, or post-vaccination is mandatory. The nature of bleeding, whether it is superficial or deep-sited, acute or recurrent, mucocutaneous, or musculoskeletal helps to differentiate between bleeding and coagulation disorders. It is important to rule out non-accidental injury (child abuse) in cases of multiple types of injuries (such as fractures, burns or bite marks), variable ages of bruises, suspicious family dynamics, unclear mechanism of injury, or disproportionate family anxiety. Family History: History of bleeding tendency, especially in maternal uncles or maternal grandfather to rule out hemophilia, history of surgical challenges in family, and history of menorrhagia in female family members, to rule out VWD or platelet function disorders. Consanguinity should be stated. Drug history: Aspirin, NSAIDs, heparin, oral anticoagulants, or chemotherapeutic agents. Social history: To rule out child abuse. It is important to know the degree of family education and the proximity of residence to health care facilities. Vaccination history: any bleeding? Menstrual history: Important in teens with VWD or platelet dysfunction.

objectives: Define failure to thrive.

Increased metabolic demand: hyperthyroidism, chronic diseases (CHF), chronic inflammatory conditions, renal failure, malignancy.
Poor absorption: celiac disease, cystic fibrosis, malabsorptive enteropathy, inflammatory bowel disease.
Poor oral intake: Inability to suck and swallow (CNS disease), GERD

topic_objectives.topic: Approach to a child with proteinuria

objectives: Recognize that proteinuria can be symptomatic or asymptomatic.
Recognize the need to include urinalysis in the physical examination of children.
Differentiate between transient and persistent proteinuria and between glomerular and tubular proteinuria.
To list the important investigations needed to reach the diagnosis.
To know that the treatment of proteinuria depends on the etiology.
Students should be able to define proteinuria by the 3 different methods: the dipstick, spot urine sample for protein to creatinine ratio, and the 24-hour collection of urinary protein.

Know that the urinary dipstick is a screening tool and needs to be confirmed by urinary protein to creatinine ratio and the gold standard test the 24hour urinary collection to quantify the amount of proteinuria. Should be able to list the different reasons for false positive and false negative proteinuria on the dipstick.

Normal protein excretion in children is defined as negative or trace in the urine dipstick, protein to creatinine ratio of less than 20mg/mmo1 (less than 60mg/mmo1 in children less than 2 years), and 24-hour protein excretion of less than or equal to 4mg/m2/hour.

Abnormal protein excretion in children is defined as more than or equal to 1+ in the urine dipstick, protein to creatinine ratio of more than 20mg/mmo1 (more than 60mg/mmol in children less than 2 years), and 24-hour protein excretion of more than 4mg/m2/hour.

Nephrotic range proteinuria in children is defined as more than or equal +2-3 in the urine dipstick, protein to creatinine ratio of more than 250mg/mmol, and 24-hour protein excretion of 40mg/m2/hour.
Know how to classify the different causes of proteinuria as follows: Intermittent (Nonpostural and postural) and persistent (Glomerular and tubular).
Exclude orthostatic proteinuria defined as early morning urine samples (supine) negative for protein, while evening urine samples (upright) may contain varying concentrations of protein.
Know the typical example of transient/benign proteinuria in the neonatal period: the Tamm-Horsfall protein that accounts for the higher levels of protein excretion in this age group

Blood pressure must be measured with the proper cuff according to the age and size of the child. Hypertension might be an indicator of underlying renal disease.

Look for clues of fluid overload such as raised jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, and edema. Also, look for reduced air entry in the bases of the lungs and evidence of ascites and scrotal or labial edema. These findings can be seen in nephritic and nephrotic syndromes.

Look for signs of systemic illnesses such as palpable rash in the extensor surfaces of the lower limbs that can be suggestive of Henoch Schoenlein. Also, look for joint swelling and erythema suggesting connective tissue disorders.
Palpable flank masses might be suggestive of polycystic kidney disease or hydronephrosis.
Students should be able to list different causes of Proteinuria:

Intermittent postural proteinuria: orthostatic proteinuria.

Persistent glomerular proteinuria: primary glomerulonephropathies (eg. minimal change disease and focal segmental glomerulonephritis) and secondary glomerulonephropathies (eg. postinfectious glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, and IgA nephropathy).
Persistent tubular proteinuria: Hereditary (eg.all causes of Fanconi syndrome such as cystinosis, galactosemia, and tyrosinemia) and Acquired (eg. Interstitial nephritis and pyelonephritis).
Symptomatic: Students should recognize that detailed investigations should be started early for children with symptoms suggestive of renal disease.

Know that renal biopsy is indicated in persistent significant unexplained proteinuria, associated hematuria, persistent complement abnormalities, evidence of connective tissue disease.
Asymptomatic: Students should know that 3-6 months follow up is required in this group until urine dipstick is negative
Students should know that investigations done for symptomatic proteinuria will need to be done if the proteinuria persists, if hematuria develops and if proteinuria worsens.

topic_objectives.topic: Approach to a child with hematuria

objectives: To learn a comprehensive approach to a child with hematuria
To avoid unnecessary and extensive workup for hematuria due to benign condition.
To identify those cases of hematuria that need advanced investigation and specific treatment.
To know when to refer these cases to a pediatric nephrologist.
Hematuria is gross hematuria that is visible dark urine or microscopic hematuria defined as the presence of at least 5 red blood cells (RBC) per microliter of urine.
To be aware of causes of dark or red color urine that are not due to the presence of RBC (False positive hematuria) like certain foods, drugs, hemoglobinuria, and myoglobinuria.

To know that in a child with dark urine due to drugs or foods urine dipstick will be negative for blood and in a child with dark urine due to hemoglobinuria and myoglobinuria urine dipstick will be positive for blood but urine microscopy will not show the presence of RBCs.

To have the knowledge that hematuria may originate from any site in the urinary system. These sites include the glomeruli, renal tubules, ureters, urinary bladder, or urethra. In other words, hematuria can be glomerular or non-glomerular in origin.
To know the differential diagnosis for glomerular and non-glomerular origin hematuria.
To understand the pathophysiology of hematuria due to glomerular and nonglomerular origin and their specific clinical presentation, workup, and treatment.

Student should be able to take a proper history to describe the hematuria as gross or microscopic and intermittent or persistent. To identify that hematuria is initial (beginning of micturition only), total (throughout the micturition phase) or terminal (at the end of micturition) as it may help determine the cause and sites of bleeding.

To take a detailed history of medications, recent foods have taken by the patient, any chronic hematological illness with chronic hemolysis or any history of muscle pain and tenderness to rule out false-positive causes of hematuria.
Recent history of trauma or strenuous exercise or chronic coagulopathy.
Abdominal or flank pain and history of stone passage to rule out renal stone diseases.

History of upper respiratory tract illness before the onset of hematuria to rule out acute glomerulonephritis or IgA nephropathy. Symptoms of systemic connective tissue disorders like oral ulcers, joint pains, skin rash.
History of dysuria, urgency, frequency, fever and flank pain to rule out urinary tract infection.

Family history of renal disease with deafness as features of Alport’s syndrome or family history of hematuria (usually microscopic) without deafness or renal failure suggest benign familial hematuria.
To look for the presence of hypertension and edema which points towards acute glomerulonephritis.
Check for the presence of skin rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers or joint swelling or tenderness as it may indicate hematuria due to systemi c lupus erythematosus or Henoch Schoenlein purpura.
Look for signs of volume overload as raised jugular venous pressure, edema, decreased air entry at the lung bases, hepatomegaly and ascites, suggestive of renal failure due to glomerulonephritis.

Abdominal examination to look for palpable kidneys seen in gross hydronephrosis, polycystic kidney disease or renal tumors. Check for costovertebral angle tenderness or suprapubic tenderness suggestive of pyelonephritis or cystitis respectively.

History: Elicit a detailed relevant history of the swelling, its duration, associated pain and relation to eating (A long history is generally associated with benign, while a short history is mostly linked to malignant, and inflammatory swellings are generally painful.
Swellings that appear while eating are mostly from salivary glands).

The commonest swelling in the neck is an enlarged lymph node commonly due to infection or secondary deposits. A history of systemic illness (malaise, fever, rigors, contact) may indicate infective cause. A history of contact with patient with tuberculosis should be elicited. A history of smoking and chronic alcohol consumption should be taken if malignancy is suspected (risk factors for aero-digestive malignancy)
A history of enlargement of nodes in other areas would indicate generalized lymphadenopathy (infective or lympho-proliferative conditions)
Elicit history of pain or ulcers in the mouth, dental caries, ENT symptoms, change of voice, ulcers or swellings over the head and face.
Dysphagia is associated with esophageal malignancy, pharyngeal pouch, thyroid with retrosternal extension.
Breast, respiratory and GI symptoms should be elicited if the swelling is in the lower lateral neck. They should also elicit history of neuro-vascular symptoms of the upper limb (cervical rib).
Propose a differential diagnosis based on the age, presentation and location of the swelling.
General: Should look for generalized lymphadenopathy, weight loss & pallor
Examination of the Neck: Describe the swelling as in other places and note its location, size, shape, surface, etc.,
Situation: Sometimes the location itself indicates the diagnosis.
Branchial cyst is along the anterior border of sternomastoid at the junction of upper and middle third. Branchial fistula is at the junction of lower and middle third.
Cystic hygroma is seen in the posterior triangle in its lower part. Other swelling in the posterior triangle are Virchow’s node, cervical rib and aneurysm of subclavian artery.
An aneurysm is along the line of carotid vessels. Carotid body tumor is at the upper level of thyroid cartilage.

From above downwards midline swellings could be, submental lymph node, sublingual dermoid, lipoma, subhyoid bursa, thyroglossal cyst, thyroid, lymph node in super sternal space, retrosternal goiter, dermoid.

An enlarged parotid salivary gland usually elevates the ear lobe. If this is the case do not forget to examine the facial nerve and carry out an intra oral examination for deeper lobe enlargement (the tonsil of the affected side will be pushed towards the midline) Swellings that move on deglutition: Thyroglossal cyst, subhyoid bursa, thyroid gland and nodes attached to larynx and trachea. Skin: Ulcers, scars (tuberculosis); sinuses (tuberculosis, osteomyelitis of jaw, actinomycosis, thyroglossal fistula or branchial fistula). Note that clinically it is difficult to differentiate a sinus from fistula. Describe the skin changes if any. Redness, edema & dilated veins.
Best palpated from behind with neck flexed slightly and turned to the side
Systematically examine the swelling
Carotid body tumor and aneurysm move transversely
Determine its relation to sternomastoid by contracting the muscle
Pulsatile (aneurysm of carotid vessels, carotid body tumor)
Swelling in the submandibular triangle could be an enlarged salivary gland (bidigitally palpable) or a lymph node.
Lymph nodes should be examined systematically (circular chain, vertical chain).

Enlarged fleshy nodes are suggestive of lymphoma. Matted liquefied nodes are adherent to skin and are suggestive of tuberculosis. Painless, firm to hard, fixed nodes are suggestive of metastatic nodes.

Examine the draining area if the lymph node is suspicious. Do not forget to remove dentures and palpate the oral cavity for induration. Base of the tongue is frequently missed. If Virchow’s node is enlarged examine the arm, breast, chest and abdomen including the testis in male patients.
A bruit may be heard in patients with aneurysm or carotid body tumor.
Examination of the upper limb in case of cervical rib: Neuro vascular exam. Adson’s test.
